meta.purpose: A descriptive comparison. Positions are summarised from each tradition's own catechisms and confessions; real churches and believers vary within every tradition.
meta.spectrumNote: The spectrum places each tradition's typical teaching between two poles. It shows difference, not better or worse.

shares.source: Pew Research Center, Global Christianity (2011), data for 2010

commonGround.text: One God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Jesus Christ, fully God and fully man
His death for our sins and bodily resurrection
Salvation by God's grace in Christ
The Bible as God's inspired word
Christ's return, the resurrection of the dead and the judgment
Baptism and the Lord's Supper, commanded by Christ

traditions.name: Roman Catholic
traditions.documents: Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992); Council of Trent; Vatican II

traditions.name: Eastern Orthodox
traditions.documents: The seven ecumenical councils; the Church Fathers; the Divine Liturgy

traditions.name: Lutheran
traditions.documents: Augsburg Confession (1530); Luther's Small Catechism; Book of Concord (1580)

traditions.name: Anglican
traditions.documents: Thirty-Nine Articles (1571); Book of Common Prayer (1662)

traditions.name: Reformed / Presbyterian
traditions.documents: Westminster Confession (1646); Heidelberg Catechism (1563); Calvin's Institutes

traditions.name: Baptist
traditions.documents: Second London Confession (1689); Baptist Faith and Message (2000)

traditions.name: Pentecostal
traditions.documents: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916)

topics.name: Authority
topics.question: Where does final authority lie?
topics.right: Scripture within Tradition, taught by the Church

catholic.text: Scripture and Sacred Tradition form one deposit of faith, interpreted with authority by the Magisterium: the Pope and the bishops in communion with him.

orthodox.text: Holy Tradition, with Scripture at its heart, is kept by the whole Church; the seven ecumenical councils and the Church Fathers carry authority.

anglican.text: Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation (Article VI); it is read alongside the early creeds, tradition and reason.

lutheran.text: Scripture is the only rule and norm; the Lutheran Confessions are held as its faithful explanation.

reformed.text: Scripture is the supreme judge in all controversies (Westminster Confession 1.10); confessions are subordinate standards.

baptist.text: Scripture is the sole authority for faith and practice; confessions are not binding creeds, and each church interprets under Christ.

pentecostal.text: Scripture is the inspired, infallible rule; the Spirit still speaks through gifts such as prophecy, always tested by Scripture.

topics.why: Every other disagreement depends on this one. When Christians read the Bible differently, who settles the question: the individual reader, the confessions of a church, or the Church’s teaching office?
topics.history: The Reformers’ “Scripture alone” (sola scriptura) challenged the medieval Church. The Council of Trent (1546) answered that the apostles’ teaching comes to us in Scripture and unwritten Tradition together. The Orthodox speak of one Holy Tradition, with Scripture at its heart.

terms.def: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith; creeds and confessions are trusted because they agree with it.
The teaching office of the Pope and the bishops in communion with him (Catholic).
The faith handed down in the whole life of the Church: Scripture, the councils, the Fathers and the liturgy (Orthodox).

topics.name: Salvation
topics.question: How is a person made right with God?
topics.right: Grace received through faith and the sacraments, renewing the whole person
topics.note: In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, stating a 'consensus in basic truths' while differences remain.

catholic.text: By grace, through faith working in love. Justification includes inner renewal and is nourished by the sacraments (Council of Trent).

orthodox.text: Salvation is theosis: union with God by grace, received through faith, the sacramental life and lifelong repentance.

anglican.text: 'We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord… by Faith, and not for our own works' (Article XI).

lutheran.text: Justified by grace alone through faith alone, for Christ's sake (Augsburg Confession IV). Good works follow as fruit.

reformed.text: Justified by faith alone; Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer, by God's sovereign grace (Westminster Confession 11).

baptist.text: Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone; believers are born again and kept by God.

pentecostal.text: Saved by grace through repentance and faith in Christ. Baptism in the Spirit is a later empowering, not a condition of salvation.

topics.why: The question that sparked the Reformation. Lutherans later called justification “the article by which the church stands or falls”.
topics.history: Luther’s 95 Theses (1517) began a dispute about indulgences that became a dispute about how a sinner is made right with God. Trent answered in 1547. In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a Joint Declaration finding a “consensus in basic truths”, while differences remain.

terms.def: Being put right with God: for Protestants a declaration, for Catholics also an inner renewal.
Christ’s righteousness credited to the believer, who is accepted for Christ’s sake (Protestant).
Becoming by grace a sharer in God’s nature, the Orthodox way of describing salvation.

topics.name: Lord's Supper
topics.question: What happens at the Lord's Supper?
topics.right: Bread and wine become Christ's body and blood

catholic.text: Transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood. The Mass makes present Christ's one sacrifice.

orthodox.text: The gifts truly become Christ's body and blood. The Church confesses the change as a mystery, without defining how.

lutheran.text: Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine.

anglican.text: A real, spiritual feeding on Christ. Article XXVIII rejects transubstantiation, but views range from Catholic to Reformed.

reformed.text: Christ is truly received, spiritually, by faith: the Spirit unites believers to him as they eat.

baptist.text: An ordinance of remembrance that proclaims Christ's death, with bread and cup as symbols of his body and blood.

pentecostal.text: Mostly memorial: a remembrance of Christ's death and a sign of fellowship until he comes.

topics.why: Jesus said “This is my body.” How literally to take it divided Catholics from Protestants, and Protestants from one another: Luther and Zwingli failed to agree at the Marburg Colloquy (1529).
topics.history: The term “transubstantiation” was used at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and defined at Trent (1551). Luther kept the real presence; Zwingli taught a memorial; Calvin a spiritual feeding. The Orthodox affirm the change without explaining how.

terms.def: The substance of bread and wine becomes Christ’s body and blood, though their appearance remains (Catholic).
Christ is truly present in the Supper, however that is explained.
The Supper is a remembrance and proclamation of Christ’s death (Zwingli, Baptists).

topics.name: Baptism
topics.question: Who is baptised, and what does baptism do?
topics.left: Believers only: a public sign of faith
topics.right: Infants too: new birth given by God

catholic.text: Infants and adults. Baptism washes away original sin and gives new birth; usually by pouring.

orthodox.text: Infants and adults, by triple immersion, followed at once by chrismation and first communion.

lutheran.text: Infants and adults. Through God's word joined to the water, baptism gives forgiveness and new birth (Small Catechism).

anglican.text: Infants and adults; a sign of regeneration by which the baptised are grafted into the Church (Article XXVII).

reformed.text: Children of believers and adult converts; a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, not saving in itself.

baptist.text: Believers only, by immersion: an act of obedience picturing death, burial and resurrection with Christ.

pentecostal.text: Believers, by immersion. Many also expect a distinct 'baptism in the Holy Spirit', marked by speaking in tongues.

topics.why: Two linked questions: should babies be baptised, and does baptism itself give new birth or does it signify a faith already there?
topics.history: Infant baptism was the common practice of the ancient church. In 1525 the Anabaptists in Zurich began baptising only believers; the Baptists followed in 1609. Pentecostals later added a distinct “baptism in the Spirit”.

terms.def: Baptism only for those old enough to confess faith, usually by immersion.
God gives new birth through baptism (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran).
Baptism marks a child of believers as belonging to God’s people, as circumcision did (Reformed).

topics.name: Sacraments
topics.question: How many sacraments are there?
topics.right: Seven sacraments, as means of grace

catholic.text: Seven: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders and marriage.

orthodox.text: The same seven 'holy mysteries' are usually listed, though the Church does not strictly fix the number.

lutheran.text: Baptism and the Lord's Supper (confession and absolution sometimes counted as a third), as true means of grace.

anglican.text: Two 'Sacraments of the Gospel'; the other five are 'commonly called Sacraments' (Article XXV).

reformed.text: Two sacraments, as signs and seals of the covenant of grace.

baptist.text: Two ordinances, kept in obedience to Christ rather than as channels of saving grace.

pentecostal.text: Two ordinances; some churches also practise foot-washing.

topics.why: Does God promise to give grace through particular rites, and which ones did Christ himself establish?
topics.history: The list of seven appears in Peter Lombard’s Sentences (c. 1150) and was defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1547). The Reformers kept the two instituted by Christ in the Gospels, baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

terms.def: An outward sign through which God gives inward grace.
A practice kept because Christ commanded it, rather than as a channel of grace (Baptist, Pentecostal).

topics.name: Church leadership
topics.question: Who leads the church?
topics.right: Bishops in succession, under a universal head

catholic.text: Bishops in apostolic succession under the Pope, the Bishop of Rome, who has universal jurisdiction.

orthodox.text: Bishops in apostolic succession; self-governing churches in communion. The Ecumenical Patriarch is 'first among equals'.

anglican.text: Bishops, priests and deacons in self-governing provinces; the Archbishop of Canterbury is a focus of unity.

lutheran.text: It varies: bishops in the Nordic churches, synods with elected leaders elsewhere.

reformed.text: Presbyterian: each church is led by elders, joined in presbyteries and general assemblies.

baptist.text: Congregational: each local church governs itself under Christ and cooperates voluntarily.

pentecostal.text: Mixed: bodies such as the Assemblies of God combine local self-government with district and national councils.

topics.why: Who has the authority to teach, to ordain ministers and to discipline: one bishop over a region, elders together, or the whole congregation?
topics.history: A single bishop leading each city’s church is attested by about 110 (Ignatius of Antioch). The Pope’s universal jurisdiction, defined at Vatican I (1870), is not accepted by the Orthodox or Protestants. Presbyterian and congregational church order arose at the Reformation.

terms.def: An unbroken line of bishops ordained by bishops back to the apostles.
Government by elders (presbyters) in councils, from the local session to a general assembly.
Each local church is self-governing under Christ.

topics.name: Mary & the saints
topics.question: How are Mary and the saints honoured?
topics.left: Honoured as examples; prayer to God alone
topics.right: Venerated, and asked to pray for us

catholic.text: Mary is venerated as Mother of God; the Immaculate Conception (1854) and Assumption (1950) are dogma. The saints are asked to intercede.

orthodox.text: Mary is the Theotokos, honoured above all saints; icons are venerated and the saints' prayers sought. The Immaculate Conception is not taught.

anglican.text: Mary is honoured and her feasts are kept; practice ranges from Anglo-Catholic devotion to Protestant restraint.

lutheran.text: Mary is honoured as Mother of God and the saints as examples, but they are not invoked (Augsburg Confession XXI).

reformed.text: Mary is blessed as the mother of the Lord; prayer is made to God alone, through Christ.

baptist.text: Mary is a model of faith. Christ is the only mediator, so prayer to the saints is not practised.

pentecostal.text: Mary is honoured as a faithful believer; prayer is made to God alone, through Christ.

topics.why: All of these churches honour Mary as the mother of Jesus. They differ on her role today and on asking saints to pray for us.
topics.history: The Council of Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos, “Mother of God”, a title most Reformers also kept. The Catholic dogmas of the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption (1950) came much later and are not shared by the Orthodox or Protestants.

terms.def: “God-bearer”: Mary bore the one person who is God, so she is Mother of God.
Honour given to saints, which Catholics and Orthodox distinguish from the worship due to God alone.
Asking someone, living or in heaven, to pray for you.

topics.name: The Old Testament
topics.question: Which books belong in the Old Testament?

catholic.text: 73 books in all: the 66 plus Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and longer Esther and Daniel (Council of Trent, 1546).

orthodox.text: The Catholic additions plus 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151.

anglican.text: 66 books. The Apocrypha is read 'for example of life', but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).

lutheran.text: 66 books. Luther's Bible printed the Apocrypha separately, as 'useful and good to read'.

reformed.text: 66 books. The Apocrypha is 'of no authority in the Church of God' (Westminster Confession 1.3).

topics.why: Which books are Scripture shapes other doctrines; prayer for the dead, for example, is supported from 2 Maccabees.
topics.history: The Greek Septuagint used by the early church contained extra books. Jerome called them apocrypha; Luther printed them separately in his 1534 Bible; Trent declared them canonical (1546). The Orthodox include a few more.

terms.def: “Second canon”: Catholic and Orthodox name for the books beyond the Hebrew Bible.
Protestant name for the same books: useful to read, but not Scripture.

topics.name: Clergy
topics.question: Who may be ordained, and may ministers marry?

catholic.text: Men only. Latin-rite priests are normally celibate; Eastern Catholic churches have married priests.

orthodox.text: Men only. Married men may become priests, but bishops are chosen from celibate monks.

anglican.text: Married clergy. Most provinces ordain women as priests, and many as bishops.

lutheran.text: Married clergy. Many Lutheran churches ordain women; some do not.

reformed.text: Married ministers and elders. Whether women are ordained varies by denomination.

baptist.text: Married pastors. Some Baptist bodies, such as the Southern Baptist Convention, keep the pastorate for men; others do not.

pentecostal.text: Married ministers. Many Pentecostal churches have credentialed women ministers from their early years.

topics.why: Two questions in one: may ministers marry, and may women be ordained?
topics.history: Married clergy were normal in the early church and remain so in the East. The Latin West required celibacy from the Second Lateran Council (1139). The Reformers allowed marriage; many Protestant churches began ordaining women in the 20th century.

terms.def: Giving up marriage for the sake of the kingdom.
Setting someone apart for ministry by the laying on of hands.

topics.name: After death
topics.question: Is there a purification after death?
topics.left: No: believers go straight to be with Christ

catholic.text: Purgatory: those who die in God's grace but are not fully purified are cleansed before heaven, helped by the prayers of the living.

orthodox.text: Prays for the departed and speaks of growth after death, but does not define a purgatory.

anglican.text: Article XXII rejects 'the Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory'; some Anglicans still pray for the departed.

lutheran.text: No purgatory: those who die in Christ rest with him, awaiting the resurrection.

reformed.text: No purgatory: believers' souls 'do immediately pass into glory' (Westminster Shorter Catechism 37).

baptist.text: No purgatory: to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord.

pentecostal.text: No purgatory: believers go to be with Christ at death.

topics.why: Do the faithful need cleansing after death, and can the prayers of the living help them?
topics.history: Prayer for the dead is ancient and still practised by the Orthodox. Purgatory was defined in the West at the Councils of Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). The Reformers rejected it together with indulgences.

terms.def: A final purification after death for those who die in God’s grace (Catholic).
Praying for the dead, which the Orthodox practise without defining purgatory.

boundary.note: This compares beliefs, not people. “The historic faith” means the faith of the creeds shared by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches. Most of the movements beyond the circle call themselves Christian; they are placed there because their teaching differs from those creeds on core points, as they themselves often say. It is not a judgement on anyone’s sincerity or worth.

tests.label: The Trinity
tests.creed: We believe in one God… and in one Lord Jesus Christ… and in the Holy Spirit (Nicene Creed)

tests.label: Jesus is fully God
tests.creed: true God from true God… of one Being with the Father

tests.label: Atoning death & bodily resurrection
tests.creed: crucified for us… on the third day he rose again

tests.label: The Bible as final revelation
tests.creed: the faith once for all delivered to the saints

tests.label: Salvation by grace through Christ
tests.creed: for us and for our salvation he came down from heaven

groups.name: Oneness Pentecostal
groups.origin: 1913–16, the 'Jesus' Name' controversy in early Pentecostalism; United Pentecostal Church International, 1945
groups.self: Apostolic Pentecostals, restoring the apostles' teaching and baptism in Jesus' name.
groups.why: It affirms Jesus' full deity, his cross and resurrection, and the Bible. But it teaches that God is a single person who appears as Father, Son and Spirit. That revives modalism, a view the early church rejected in the 3rd century. Of all the groups here, its standing is the most debated.
groups.affirms: Jesus is the one true God in the flesh; his atoning death and bodily resurrection; the 66-book Bible.

trinity.text: God is one person who reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, not three persons.

deity.text: Jesus is fully God (the one God incarnate) and fully man.

cross.text: Affirms Christ's atoning death and bodily resurrection.

scripture.text: The 66-book Bible is the inspired, final authority.

grace.text: Grace through faith, expressed in repentance, baptism in Jesus' name, and the gift of the Spirit with tongues.

groups.name: Latter-day Saints (Mormon)
groups.self: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: the restoration of the church Jesus founded.
groups.why: It teaches that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three separate beings, and that the Father has a physical body. It also adds new scriptures and continuing revelation. Both depart from the Nicene definition of God and the closed canon. In 2001 the Catholic Church ruled that Latter-day Saint baptism is not valid Christian baptism for these reasons.
groups.affirms: Jesus as Saviour and Redeemer; his atonement and bodily resurrection; the Bible as scripture.

trinity.text: The Godhead is three separate beings; the Father 'has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's' (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22).

deity.text: Jesus is divine and the Son of God, but a separate being from the Father rather than 'of one Being' with him.

cross.text: Christ's atonement (in Gethsemane and on the cross) and his bodily resurrection.

scripture.text: An open canon: the Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price stand beside the Bible, with continuing revelation through living prophets.

grace.text: Salvation through Christ's grace together with covenants, ordinances (including temple ordinances) and obedience.

groups.name: Iglesia ni Cristo
groups.self: The Church of Christ: the true church re-established in the last days.
groups.why: Like the 4th-century Arians, it teaches that Christ is not God by nature, and it rejects the Trinity. It also holds that membership in its own church is needed for salvation.
groups.affirms: Christ as Son of God, Saviour and Lord; his death and resurrection; the Bible as the basis of faith.

trinity.text: Only the Father is the one true God; the Trinity is rejected.

deity.text: Christ is a man, the Son of God, made Lord and Saviour by God, but not God by nature.

cross.text: Christ died for the Church and rose again.

scripture.text: The Bible is the basis of faith, as taught through Felix Manalo, regarded as God's last messenger, and his successors.

grace.text: Membership in the Iglesia ni Cristo is necessary for salvation.

groups.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
groups.origin: 1870s, the Bible Student movement of Charles Taze Russell
groups.self: Worshippers of Jehovah who follow Christ, restoring first-century Christianity.
groups.why: It revives the Arian view that the Son is a created being, which the Council of Nicaea rejected in 325. It denies the Trinity and the Spirit's personhood, and holds that Jesus was raised as a spirit, not in his body.
groups.affirms: Jesus as the Son of God, Messiah and ransom; the 66-book Bible; Jesus' coming kingdom.

trinity.text: Only Jehovah is Almighty God; the holy spirit is his active force, not a person.

deity.text: Jesus is God's first creation, identified with the archangel Michael before he became human: 'a god' in their translation of John 1:1.

cross.text: Jesus' death is a ransom for mankind, but he was raised as an immortal spirit, not in his body.

scripture.text: The 66 books, read in the New World Translation as explained by the Governing Body.

grace.text: Salvation through faith in the ransom, with obedience and loyalty to Jehovah's organisation.

groups.name: Christadelphians
groups.origin: 1848, John Thomas, USA and Britain (the name “Christadelphian” from 1864)
groups.self: Brothers and sisters in Christ, returning to the beliefs of the first-century believers.
groups.why: Like the 16th-century Socinians, it holds that Jesus did not exist before his birth and is not God, and that the Holy Spirit is God’s power rather than a person. That rejects the Trinity as defined at Nicaea and Constantinople. It affirms Jesus’ death and bodily resurrection strongly.
groups.affirms: Jesus as the sinless Son of God and Messiah; his death and bodily resurrection; his return to set up God’s kingdom on earth; the Bible as the only authority.

trinity.text: God is one, the Father; the Holy Spirit is his power, not a person.

deity.text: Jesus is the Son of God, born of Mary, who did not exist before his birth; he is not God.

cross.text: Affirms Jesus’ death and bodily resurrection, understanding his sacrifice as representative rather than substitutionary.

scripture.text: The Bible alone, without any other authoritative writings.

grace.text: Salvation by grace through faith, with right belief and baptism by immersion essential; the faithful are raised at Christ’s return.

groups.name: Christian Science
groups.self: Church of Christ, Scientist: rediscovering Jesus' healing Christianity.
groups.why: It reinterprets God as impersonal divine Mind and separates the man Jesus from 'the Christ'. It denies that his death atoned for sin, and it reads the Bible through Science and Health.
groups.affirms: Jesus' virgin birth, his healing ministry, and the Bible as inspired.

trinity.text: God is infinite Mind, Spirit, Life, Truth and Love; the 'trinity' is Life, Truth and Love, not three persons.

deity.text: Jesus is the human man; 'the Christ' is the divine idea he expressed. Jesus is not God.

cross.text: The crucifixion showed divine Love rather than paying for sin; sin, sickness and death are ultimately unreal.

scripture.text: The Bible, together with Eddy's Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures as its interpreter.

grace.text: Salvation is freedom from the belief in sin, sickness and death, through understanding divine Science.

groups.name: Unification Church
groups.origin: 1954, Sun Myung Moon, Seoul; now the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification
groups.self: Completing God’s plan of restoration through the “True Parents”, Sun Myung Moon and Hak Ja Han.
groups.why: Its scripture, the Divine Principle, teaches that Jesus’ crucifixion was not God’s original plan and won only spiritual salvation, and that the work is completed by Sun Myung Moon as the Lord of the Second Advent. It adds a new revelation and a new saviour figure, and it departs from every core belief.
groups.affirms: Jesus as a son of God and a saviour; the Bible as revelation; a strong emphasis on family.

trinity.text: The Trinity is reinterpreted through God’s “dual characteristics” and the True Parents, not three eternal persons.

deity.text: Jesus is a perfected man, one with God in purpose, but not God himself.

cross.text: The crucifixion was not God’s original will and brought only spiritual salvation; physical salvation awaits the Lord of the Second Advent.

scripture.text: The Divine Principle is new revelation that completes the Bible.

grace.text: Full salvation comes through the True Parents and the Blessing marriage ceremony.

groups.name: Unitarian Universalism
groups.origin: 1961, merger of the Unitarian and Universalist movements
groups.self: A liberal religion with Jewish and Christian roots, drawing on many sources, with no required creed.
groups.why: It no longer presents itself as a Christian church and has no creed, so it meets none of the core tests, though some members do call themselves Christian.
groups.affirms: Jesus is widely admired as a moral teacher.

trinity.text: Its Unitarian roots reject the Trinity; no belief about God is required.

deity.text: Jesus is honoured as a teacher; his deity is not affirmed.

cross.text: No belief in the atonement or the resurrection is required.

scripture.text: The Bible is one source among many, alongside other traditions, science and experience.

grace.text: From its Universalist heritage: no one is finally lost, and no single way of salvation is taught.

groups.name: Islam
groups.self: Submission to the one God. Islam honours Isa (Jesus) as a great prophet and the Messiah, born of the virgin Mary.
groups.why: Islam does not claim to be Christian. It honours Jesus more than any other religion outside Christianity, but denies his deity, his crucifixion and the Trinity.
groups.affirms: Jesus' virgin birth, his miracles, his title of Messiah, and his return.

trinity.text: God is absolutely one: 'do not say "Three"' (Qur'an 4:171).

deity.text: Jesus is a prophet and the Messiah, but not divine and not God's son (Qur'an 5:116–117; 112).

cross.text: 'They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him' (Qur'an 4:157); God raised him up to himself.

scripture.text: The Qur'an is God's final revelation; earlier scriptures are held to have been altered.

grace.text: Salvation through God's mercy, faith and righteous deeds, without an atoning sacrifice.

confessed.label: Confessed
confessed.note: Officially adopted, or recited in worship

content.label: Agrees with it
content.note: Holds its teaching, though the tradition does not use creeds formally

unused.label: Not used
unused.note: Shares the faith, but does not use this text

rejects.label: Rejects
rejects.note: Rejects this creed or its teaching

notes.apostles: A Western baptismal creed. The Eastern and Oriental Orthodox share its faith but do not use the text.
notes.nicene: The most widely shared creed: confessed by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and most Protestant churches. Every movement outside the boundary rejects its definition of the Son as “of one substance with the Father”.
notes.chalcedon: The line that divides the families inside the boundary: the Oriental Orthodox did not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451), though recent dialogues have found that both sides confess the same Christ in different words.
notes.athanasian: A Latin creed of the West, with its warning clauses. The East does not use it, though it shares the faith it defines.

families.name: Catholic
families.about: One church in communion with the Pope, made up of 24 self-governing (sui iuris) churches: the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic churches. They share one faith and the Pope’s authority, but keep their own liturgies, languages and customs.
families.self: The one Church founded by Christ, subsisting in the Catholic Church.
families.why: Confesses the Nicene Creed in full. Its differences with Orthodox and Protestant churches lie within the shared faith: see the Traditions tab.
families.creedNote: The Latin Church recites the Nicene Creed with “and the Son”; several Eastern Catholic churches leave it out.

members.name: Latin Church
members.about: The Roman Catholic Church of the West, by far the largest, worshipping in the Roman rite.

members.name: Maronite Catholic Church
members.about: Based mainly in Lebanon, worshipping with an ancient Syriac liturgy.

members.name: Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
members.about: Follows the Byzantine liturgy of the Orthodox East while in full communion with the Pope (since the Union of Brest, 1596).

members.name: Syro-Malabar Church
members.about: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala, India, who trace their faith to the apostle Thomas; they worship in the East Syriac tradition.

families.name: Eastern Orthodox
families.about: A communion of self-governing churches, organised largely by nation and language rather than by doctrine. They share one faith and the Byzantine liturgy; the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople is “first among equals”.
families.self: The undivided Church of the apostles and the councils, kept unchanged.
families.why: Confesses the Nicene Creed (without the Western 'and the Son'). Its differences lie within the shared faith: see the Traditions tab.
families.creedNote: Recites the Nicene Creed in its original form, without the Western “and the Son”.

members.name: Russian Orthodox Church
members.about: The largest Orthodox church by membership.

members.name: Greek Orthodox Church
members.about: The Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople and the Church of Greece, rooted in the Greek-speaking churches of the New Testament.

members.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
members.about: A major national church of Eastern Europe, self-governing since St Sava in 1219.

members.name: Romanian Orthodox Church
members.about: One of the largest Orthodox churches, and the main church of Romania and Moldova.

families.name: Oriental Orthodox
families.about: The ancient churches that did not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451). They speak of one united divine-human nature of Christ, following St Cyril of Alexandria. Their communion is ancient and largely national.
families.self: The churches of the first three councils, keeping the faith of St Cyril of Alexandria.
families.why: Confesses the Nicene Creed and the Trinity. It parted from the rest of the church over how to describe Christ’s natures at Chalcedon (451), not over whether he is fully God and fully man; recent dialogues have found that both sides confess the same Christ in different words.
families.creedNote: Recites the Nicene Creed without “and the Son”; does not accept the Chalcedonian Definition.

members.name: Coptic Orthodox Church
members.about: The church of Egypt, which traces its founding to St Mark, and the largest Christian church in the Middle East.

members.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
members.about: One of Africa’s oldest churches, with distinctive customs and the widest biblical canon, which includes Enoch and Jubilees.

members.name: Armenian Apostolic Church
members.about: The church of Armenia, traditionally the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion, in 301.

families.name: Protestant
families.about: Churches shaped by the Reformation from 1517: Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone. Because each reads Scripture for itself, this is the family with the most denominations. They share the creeds’ faith, though some do not recite creeds at all.
families.self: Churches reformed by the Scriptures: grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone.
families.why: Affirms the Trinity and the content of the Nicene Creed, even where creeds are not recited. Its differences with Catholic and Orthodox lie within the shared faith: see the Traditions tab.
families.creedNote: Varies by denomination: the Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions formally receive the three “ecumenical” creeds; Baptist, Pentecostal and other free churches hold their teaching without reciting them.

members.name: Lutheran
members.examples: Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA), Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod (LCMS)
members.about: From Martin Luther’s reform in Germany. The Book of Concord (1580) receives the three ecumenical creeds.

members.name: Reformed / Presbyterian
members.examples: Presbyterian Church (USA), Dutch Reformed churches, Church of Scotland
members.about: From Zwingli and Calvin in Switzerland. The Belgic Confession (Article 9) receives the three creeds.

members.name: Anglican / Episcopal
members.examples: Church of England, The Episcopal Church (USA), Church of Nigeria
members.about: From the English Reformation. Article VIII of the Thirty-Nine Articles: the three creeds “ought thoroughly to be received and believed”.

members.name: Methodist
members.examples: United Methodist Church, African Methodist Episcopal Church
members.about: From John and Charles Wesley’s revival in 18th-century England. The Apostles’ and Nicene Creeds are said in worship.

members.name: Baptist
members.examples: Southern Baptist Convention, American Baptist Churches USA, National Baptist Convention
members.about: Believers’ baptism and self-governing congregations. Baptists hold the creeds’ teaching but prefer confessions of faith to fixed creeds.

members.name: Pentecostal / Charismatic
members.examples: Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ; charismatic church networks such as Hillsong and Bethel
members.about: From the Azusa Street revival (1906), stressing the gifts of the Spirit. Trinitarian, but rarely recites creeds.

members.name: Anabaptist
members.about: The Radical Reformation’s heirs, known for believers’ baptism, nonviolence and simple living. Their confessions (such as Dordrecht, 1632) teach the Trinity.

members.name: Seventh-day Adventist
members.origin: 1863, from the Millerite movement in New England (Ellen G. White, Joseph Bates, James White)
members.self: A Protestant church that keeps the seventh-day Sabbath and proclaims Christ’s soon return.
members.why: It confesses the Trinity, the full deity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, salvation by grace through faith, and the Bible as the standard for all teaching (28 Fundamental Beliefs). It is therefore usually placed inside, with distinctive doctrines on the edge: Saturday worship, Christ’s ministry in the heavenly sanctuary since 1844, the soul’s unconsciousness until the resurrection, and the prophetic gift of Ellen White. Some critics have counted it outside; after long study the evangelical scholar Walter Martin concluded it is a Christian denomination, though one with errors in his view.
members.affirms: Everything at the core. The differences are Protestant-style disagreements about the Sabbath, the end times and the state of the dead.

trinity.text: “There is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a unity of three coeternal Persons” (Fundamental Belief 2).

deity.text: Jesus is “forever truly God” who became truly man (Fundamental Belief 4).

cross.text: Christ’s substitutionary, atoning death and his bodily resurrection.

scripture.text: The 66 books are “the standard by which all teaching and experience must be tested”; Ellen White’s writings are honoured as prophetic but subordinate to the Bible (Fundamental Belief 18).

grace.text: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ; Sabbath-keeping is the fruit of salvation, not its cause.

members.about: Keeps the Sabbath on Saturday and stresses Christ’s soon return.

members.name: Grace Communion
members.origin: Founded in the 1930s by Herbert W. Armstrong as the Worldwide Church of God; renamed Grace Communion International in 2009
members.self: An evangelical denomination, transformed by grace from its Armstrong-era teaching.
members.why: A rare case of a movement crossing the boundary. Under Herbert Armstrong it denied the Trinity and taught that keeping Old Testament law was needed for salvation. After his death in 1986 its leaders studied the Bible afresh: the church accepted the Trinity in 1993, embraced salvation by grace, and now fully agrees with the statement of faith of the National Association of Evangelicals. It shows that the boundary is about teaching, which can change.
members.affirms: Everything at the core, since the reforms of the 1990s.

deity.text: Jesus is fully God and fully human.

cross.text: Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection.

scripture.text: The Bible as the final authority, read in agreement with the evangelical statement of faith.

grace.text: Salvation by grace through faith (under Armstrong: law-keeping was required).

members.examples: Grace Communion International (formerly the Worldwide Church of God)
members.about: A movement that crossed the boundary: it embraced the Trinity in 1993.
